subject: system-design
title: Blob / Object Store
summary: A store for large unstructured objects addressed by key in a flat namespace of buckets — durable, massively scalable, and deliberately simple.

blocks.text: A blob or object store holds large, unstructured objects — images, video, backups, logs, model weights — that don't fit neatly in a database row. You address each object by a key inside a bucket, and the store hands back the bytes. Amazon S3 is the canonical example, and the same design underlies most cloud object storage.

Objects live in a flat namespace: a bucket is a container, and within it every object has a unique key. There are no real directories — a key like photos/2024/cat.jpg just looks hierarchical; the slashes are part of the name. Alongside the bytes, each object carries metadata (content type, size, custom tags) that the store indexes for listing and lookup.

Object stores are built to almost never lose data. They achieve this by replicating each object across multiple machines and often multiple data centers, or by using erasure coding — splitting an object into data and parity fragments so it can be rebuilt from a subset. Erasure coding gives the same durability as replication at far lower storage overhead, which matters at petabyte scale.

Because objects are independent and addressed by key, the store partitions them across a huge fleet and scales by adding machines. There are no joins or cross-object transactions to coordinate, so capacity and throughput grow nearly linearly. This is why object stores comfortably hold trillions of objects and exabytes of data.
How it differs from files and databases

items: Unlike a file system: a flat key namespace, no directory tree, and objects written and read whole rather than seeked and edited in place.
Accessed over HTTP APIs (GET/PUT by key), not mounted as a POSIX volume with locking.
Unlike a database: no rich queries — you fetch by key, you don't SELECT by attributes.
No cross-object transactions, and often eventually consistent — a read just after a write may briefly see stale data.

blocks.title: Blob store or database?
blocks.text: Reach for a blob store when the payload is large and opaque and you fetch it whole by an id — images, videos, files, backups. Keep it in a database when you need to query, filter, join, or transactionally update the data. A common pattern is both: store the blob in the object store and keep its key plus searchable metadata in the database.

The object store earns its place by doing one thing extremely well: storing and serving huge volumes of unstructured data cheaply and durably. Pair it with a CDN to serve those objects fast, and with a database to make them findable, and you have the backbone of most media-heavy systems.
